title: Pearson correlation
biology: Evolutionary biologists measure wing and tail lengths in adult birds from a single population.
design: Each independent bird contributes one pair of continuous traits.
data_characteristics: Strength of a linear association is the target
question: Are wing and tail lengths linearly associated in this population?
null: The population Pearson correlation is zero.
assumptions: A linear pattern with no dominating outliers
Classical inference assumes approximately bivariate-normal observations
parametric: Regression models a directional mean response and covariates
Transform traits when a log-scale association is the question
nonparametric: A bootstrap interval can retain Pearson correlation as the target

plot_args.note: Choose the two traits whose association is of interest
Display every bird while limiting overlap
Use a filled symbol with a contrasting outline
Use trait names and measurement units

practice: Would swapping wing and tail in cor.test change r? Would it leave a regression slope unchanged?
code_simulate:
set.seed(1112)
wing <- rnorm(45, 75, 5)
tail <- 15 + .55 * wing + rnorm(45, 0, 3.5)
d <- data.frame(bird = 1:45, wing_mm = wing, tail_mm = tail)
write.csv(d, file.path(output_dir, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
code_plot:
p <- ggplot(d, aes(wing_mm, tail_mm)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "#246A73", color = "white", size = 3.5, alpha = .85) +
  labs(x = "Wing length (mm)", y = "Tail length (mm)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 18)
print(p)
code_analysis:
fit <- cor.test(d$wing_mm, d$tail_mm, method = "pearson",
                alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = .95)
generating_model: 45 independent wing lengths are Normal(75, 5 SD). Tail length is 15 + 0.55 times wing length + independent Normal(0, 3.5 SD) noise.
generating_truth: The generating population Pearson correlation is 0.55*5 / sqrt((0.55*5)^2 + 3.5^2), approximately 0.618. It is not the observed sample correlation.
teaching_point: Correlation describes linear association symmetrically; causal direction and a slope are separate questions.
